units.text: **Introduction to Part 9:** Islam did not come to be an isolated spiritual rite, nor a devotional system confined to the mosque, but came as comprehensive guidance, organizing the human being’s relationship with his Lord, with himself, with others, and with the world around him.

With the complexity of contemporary life, and the intertwining of politics, economics, science, and technology, the question renews itself: does Islam possess a vision for modern life? The answer is neither a defence nor a justification, but a historical and religious truth: that Islam is fit for every time and place, because it engages with the human being, whether male or female, young or old, slave or free, rich or poor, ruler or ruled, learned or ignorant, resident or traveller, before it engages with particulars. This Part contains four chapters and a conclusion.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 1: Islam and Knowledge
chapters.partEn: Part 9: Islam and the System of Contemporary Life

units.text: From the very first verse revealed, Islam placed knowledge at the heart of its civilizational project. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“Read in the name of your Lord who created”* (Al-’Alaq 96:1).

Allah, the Exalted, also says: *“Say, ‘Are those who know equal to those who do not know?’”* (Az-Zumar 39:9), and He, the Exalted, says: *“Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge”* (Fatir 35:28).
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.”* (Reported by Ibn Majah in his Sunan, and graded sound by the scholars.)

Imam Al-Ghazali (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “Knowledge is the root of happiness, and from it deeds spring forth.” (See: *Ihya’ ’Ulum Al-Din* by Imam Al-Ghazali.) This means knowledge is the root of happiness, and righteous deeds spring from correct knowledge, and it affirms the importance of knowledge in the reform of the self and the improvement of one’s deeds.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Religion does not oppose sound knowledge; rather, it bears witness to it and guides it.” (See: *Majmu’ Al-Fatawa* by Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.) This means: the religion of Islam does not conflict with sound knowledge but bears witness to it and guides it toward the truth, and it affirms the importance of harmony between sound knowledge and the religion of Islam.
Islam, then, does not fear knowledge, nor is it hostile to reason, but disciplines knowledge with values.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 2: Islam and the Economy
chapters.partEn: Part 9: Islam and the System of Contemporary Life

units.text: Islam did not leave wealth without direction, nor the economy without ethics. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world”* (Al-Qasas 28:77).
Allah, the Exalted, also says: *“But Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden interest”* (Al-Baqarah 2:275).
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“The truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful, and the martyrs.”* (Reported by Al-Tirmidhi.)

Imam Ibn Khaldun (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Transactions in the Shari’ah are built upon securing benefit and repelling harm.” (See: *Al-Muqaddimah* by Ibn Khaldun.) This statement affirms the importance of taking public interests into account, and of avoiding harm, within Islamic law.
The economy in Islam, then, is production without oppression, earning without exploitation, and mutual solidarity that does not efface the individual.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 3: Islam and Society
chapters.partEn: Part 9: Islam and the System of Contemporary Life

units.text: Islam came to build a cohesive society founded upon justice, mercy, and responsibility. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives”* (An-Nahl 16:90).
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“The best of people are those most beneficial to people.”* (Reported by Al-Tabarani.)
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock.”* (Agreed upon.)

Imam Ibn ’Ashur (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The greatest purpose of the Shari’ah is the preservation of the order of the nation.” (See: *Maqasid Al-Shari’ah Al-Islamiyyah* by Ibn ’Ashur.) This statement affirms the importance of achieving social stability and order in the life of the nation.
Society in Islam, then, is not a collection of isolated individuals, but a network of mutual solidarity and shared responsibility.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 4: Islam in a Changing World
chapters.partEn: Part 9: Islam and the System of Contemporary Life

units.text: Among the characteristics of Islam is that it unites the fixity of its principles with the flexibility of its means. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“So remain upright as you have been commanded”* (Hud 11:112).
The Prophet ﷺ said to the Companions: *“You are more knowledgeable in the affairs of your worldly life.”* (Reported by Muslim.)

Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The Shari’ah is justice entire, mercy entire, and wisdom entire.” (See: *I’lam Al-Muwaqqi’in ’an Rabb Al-’Alamin* by Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim.) This statement affirms the importance of understanding the Shari’ah in realizing the public interest and justice.

Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “The purposes are fixed, while the means change with the changing of the times.” (See: *Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-Shari’ah* by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This means: the fundamental purposes of the Shari’ah are fixed, but the means of realizing them change according to time and circumstance, and this statement affirms the importance of accounting for changing conditions, and of adapting the means to realize the purposes of the Shari’ah.
Islam, then, does not clash with the age, nor dissolve within it, but directs it by the highest values.

chapters.headingEn: Conclusion of Part 9
chapters.partEn: Part 9: Islam and the System of Contemporary Life

units.text: Islam is a comprehensive vision, a system for living, and a civilizational project. When Islam is understood in its entirety, the illusory conflict with the age dissolves, religiosity turns into a force of construction, and religion recovers its role in guiding the human being.
From this understanding we move to the final question: how do we transform this awareness into practical action?

chapters.headingEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action
chapters.partEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action

units.text: **Introduction to Part 10:** the crisis of the nation today does not lie in a shortage of texts, nor in the obscurity of revelation, nor in the scarcity of exhortation, but in the gap between what we know and what we live.

How many a Muslim memorizes the verses of the Qur’an, repeats the Prophetic hadiths, and performs the religious rites, and yet this is never reflected in his character, his dealings, or his decisions.

For this reason, the transition from understanding to action is the true challenge of contemporary religiosity, and it is the true measure of the fruit of faith. This Part contains four chapters and a conclusion.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 1: A Crisis of Application, Not a Crisis of Text
chapters.partEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action

units.text: Revelation is complete, guidance is clear, but the disorder lies in its implementation. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favour upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion”* (Al-Ma’idah 5:3).

Allah, the Exalted, also says: *“[This is] a blessed Book which We have revealed to you, [O Muhammad], that they might reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding would be reminded”* (Sad 38:29).
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray after me: the Book of Allah.”* (Reported by Muslim.)

Imam Malik (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “The latter part of this nation will not be set right except by that which set right its earlier part.” (See: *Al-I’tisam* by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This means: the reform of the latter part of this nation lies in returning to the way of the righteous predecessors, and this statement affirms the importance of following the method of the predecessors in reforming the nation.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The obligation is to follow the texts with a correct understanding of them and their proper application to reality.” (See: *Majmu’ Al-Fatawa* by Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.) This means it is obligatory upon Muslims to follow the religious texts of the Qur’an and Sunnah with a correct understanding of them, and this affirms the importance of understanding the texts according to their linguistic and legal significations.
The crisis, then, is not in the text, but in its partial understanding, or in its selective application, that is, its application in some instances and not in others.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 2: The Muslim Individual and the Building of Reality
chapters.partEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action

units.text: Change always begins with the individual, not with slogans, but with practical commitment. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves”* (Ar-Ra’d 13:11).
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer.”* (Reported by Muslim.)
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“The best of you is the best of you to his family.”* (Reported by Al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan, and Al-Darimi in his Musnad.)

Imam Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Allah is worshipped by nothing more excellent than an understanding that bears fruit in action.” (See: *Al-Faqih wa’l-Mutafaqqih* by Al-Khatib Al-Baghdadi.) This statement indicates the importance of acting upon knowledge, and that understanding which bears no fruit in action is of no benefit to its possessor.
The Muslim individual, then, is a project of reform, a point of departure, and a silent model, and if the individual is set right, society is built upon that foundation.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 3: From Individual Piety to Collective Responsibility
chapters.partEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action

units.text: Islam is not content with a selfish religiosity, nor with worship isolated from the concerns of the nation. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“And cooperate in righteousness and piety”* (Al-Ma’idah 5:2). The Prophet ﷺ said: *“The believers, in their mutual love and mercy, are like a single body: if the head complains, the rest of it responds with sleeplessness and fever.”* (Agreed upon.)

Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “The Shari’ah came to establish the interests of the community, not merely of individuals.” (See: *Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-Shari’ah* and *Maqasid Al-Shari’ah*, both by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This statement shows that Islamic law aims to realize the interests of the community and the nation, not merely of individuals.

Ibn ’Ashur (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “Collective responsibility is an authentic purpose within Islam.” (See: *Maqasid Al-Shari’ah Al-Islamiyyah* and *Usul Al-Nizam Al-Ijtima’i fi Al-Islam*, both by Ibn ’Ashur.) This statement shows that Islam places great emphasis on the importance of the nation’s collective responsibility.
True religiosity, then, builds institutions, reforms systems, confronts corruption, and carries the concerns of the nation.

chapters.headingEn: Chapter 4: How Do We Restore Religion’s Effect on Life?
chapters.partEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action

units.text: Restoring religion’s effect on the daily life of the nation is achieved neither through confrontation nor through isolation, but through awareness and shared action together:

1. **A purposive understanding.** Al-Shatibi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “Whoever does not understand the purposes of the Shari’ah errs in applying it.” (See: *Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-Shari’ah* and *Maqasid Al-Shari’ah*, both by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This statement affirms the importance of understanding the purposes of the Shari’ah in applying Islamic rulings.
2. **A practical example.** The Prophet ﷺ said: *“I was only sent to perfect noble character.”* (Reported by Imam Ahmad.)
3. **Institutional action.** Allah, the Exalted, says: *“Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as though they are a solid structure”* (As-Saff 61:4).

4. **Patience and gradualism.** Allah, the Exalted, says: *“So be patient, [O Muhammad], as were those of determination among the messengers”* (Al-Ahqaf 46:35). Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “Religion is a continuous work, not a series of temporary leaps.” (See: *Madarij Al-Salikin* and *Al-Fawa’id*, both by Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim.) This statement shows that the religion of Islam is not merely a set of temporary acts, but continuous, unceasing work, until death, in accordance with Allah’s saying: *“And worship your Lord until there comes to your certainty [i.e., death]”* (Al-Hijr 15:99).

chapters.headingEn: Conclusion of Part 10
chapters.partEn: Part 10: From Understanding to Action

units.text: Religion is not merely information to be memorized, but a commitment; it is not merely rites, but a responsibility. When the Muslim moves from conscious understanding to sincere action, and from individual piety to a positive effect upon society, religion recovers its influence, its dignity, and its civilizational role.

chapters.headingEn: Conclusion

units.heading: The Path to Allah, Glorified and Exalted: Clarity of Understanding of the Sacred Texts, and Sincerity of Collective Action
units.text: The path to Allah is neither obscure, nor complicated, nor confined to an elite few apart from the rest of humanity, that is, reserved for some to the exclusion of others, but is, rather, a path of clear waymarks, whose method is plain, and which sincere hearts, possessed of conscious minds and firm deeds, may walk.

This religion has taught us that nearness to Allah is not measured by an abundance of slogans, nor by the sharpness of one’s rhetoric, nor by the inflation of disagreements, but is measured by a precise scale: the sincerity of faith, the soundness of deed, and benefit brought to Allah’s creation. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds…”* (Al-Buruj 85:11), He never once separated faith from deed, nor made either stand without the other.
The Prophet ﷺ said: *“Indeed, Allah does not look at your outward forms, nor at your bodies, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds.”* (Reported by Muslim.)
The heart, then, is the point of departure, and the deed is the proof, and the path is not to be walked by intentions alone, nor by deeds devoid of awareness.

This book has attempted to reorder our relationship with religion, not to alter its essence, but to remove what has clouded our understanding, and what has accumulated, in practice, of rigidity or hollowness, affirming that:
1. Monotheism is the liberation of the human being, before it is a doctrinal or verbal concept.
2. The acts of worship are instruments for building a conscious human being, not mere ritual performance.
3. Prayer is the bond of life, not bodily movements or verbal utterances.
4. Zakat is an economy of mercy, not merely the payment of taxes or the giving away of money.
5. Fasting is a school of the will, not merely the abandonment of food, drink, and appetite.
6. Hajj is a declaration of nationhood, not a commercial journey, nor an inspection tour, nor a mere excursion.
7. Islam is a comprehensive system for life, not a daily or yearly ceremony.
8. True religiosity is a transition from understanding to action, not merely the retention of information or understanding alone.

Imam Ibn Al-Qayyim (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “Religion, in its entirety, is character; whoever surpasses you in character has surpassed you in religion.” (See this statement in three of Ibn Al-Qayyim’s books: *Madarij Al-Salikin*, *Al-Fawa’id*, and *Tahdhib Madarij Al-Salikin*.) This statement shows that the religion of Islam encompasses every dimension of life, and that character is the very foundation of religion.

Imam Al-Shatibi (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: “The Shari’ah was established only for the benefit of [Allah’s] servants, in this life and the next”, end of his statement, meaning in this world and the Hereafter. (See: *Al-Muwafaqat fi Usul Al-Shari’ah* and *Maqasid Al-Shari’ah*, both by Imam Al-Shatibi.) This statement shows that Islamic law aims to realize the benefit of human beings, in this world and the Hereafter.

The path to Allah is not a flight from reality, nor an isolation from the world, nor a blind clash with the age, but an awareness of revelation, an understanding of reality, and a wisdom in application. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“And thus We have made you a just, balanced (median) community”* (Al-Baqarah 2:143), balanced in understanding, balanced in conduct, balanced in engaging with life.

Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: “The Shari’ah is founded upon justice, mercy, benefit, and wisdom.” (See: *Majmu’ Al-Fatawa* and *Al-Siyasah Al-Shar’iyyah*, both by Shaykh Al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.) This statement shows that Islamic law is founded upon the principles of justice, mercy, benefit, and wisdom.

Dear reader, this book does not ask of you that you become an ideal, nor that you change all at once, but invites you to a sincere beginning, a clear direction, and a steady step, for Allah does not look at the speed of one’s course, but at its sincerity. The Prophet ﷺ said: *“The most beloved deeds to Allah are those most consistent, even if small.”* (Agreed upon.)
And in closing: if we are right, it is from Allah alone; and if we have erred, and no doubt there is error in it, it is from ourselves and from Satan, and Allah and His Messenger are innocent of it.

We ask Allah, the Exalted, to make this work sincerely for His noble sake, to benefit by it its author, its reader, and whoever helped in its dissemination, and to make it a building block in the construction of a rightly guided awareness of faith, and a practical proof that Islam has never been a burden upon life, but has always been a path for it. Allah, the Exalted, says: *“And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways. And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good”* (Al-’Ankabut 29:69).
All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all the worlds.

chapters.headingEn: General Summary of the Book

units.text: *The Balanced Scale: A Contemporary Reading of Islam, and a Renewal of Religion’s Effect on Life*

This book proceeds from a central premise: that the crisis of Muslims today is not a crisis of religion, but a crisis of understanding and application of it, for the text has not changed, and revelation remains preserved, but reality has been transformed, and the variables of reality have multiplied.

**Part 1, Introduction to the Book: An Age of Transformations.** This Part affirms that understanding religion in an age of transformation requires a renewal of understanding, not a renewal of religion itself, and confirms that stagnation freezes religion within the moulds of its own history, while dissolution empties it of the essence of its message; and it presents Islam as the religion of innate human nature and reason together, balancing between fixity and movement, between discipline and flexibility.

**Part 2, Monotheism: The Centre of the Whole Structure.** The book presents monotheism not as a mere doctrinal, verbal concept, but as that which liberates the human being from servitude to creation and makes him a servant of Allah alone; the two testimonies of faith are not a verbal formula, but a way of life; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is not merely a conveyor of legislation, but the one who connects revelation’s guidance to practical action in reality.

units.heading: Part 3, Faith: Between Its Attachment to Knowledge and Its Attachment to Submission.
units.text: **Part 4, Acts of Worship: Between Form and Function.** The book clarifies that acts of worship were legislated to build the balanced human being, and that measuring their soundness by their behavioural effect is one of the greatest signs of formal religiosity, whereas true worship is an inward expression, not a ritual detached from life.

**Part 5, Prayer: The Bond of Life.** The book presents prayer as the balance of one’s daily faith, and a school of discipline and self-mastery, and the book uncovers that a false sense of futility is often the cause of a person’s aversion to worship if the awareness of its wisdom and purpose is lacking.

**Part 6, Zakat: An Economy of Mercy.** The book demonstrates that wealth is a trust, not an act of ownership; that zakat is a tool of justice, addressed to society, not merely to the individual; and that mutual solidarity is the foundation for achieving social balance, and the key to civilizational stability.

**Part 7, Fasting: Rebuilding the Human Being.** The book presents fasting as a school for training the will and self-restraint, and resisting consumerism and appetite, and affirms that leaving Ramadan without any real change is a warning sign requiring a review of one’s understanding of the fast’s true purpose.

**Part 8, Hajj: The Nation in a Single Scene.** The book presents Hajj as a rite that unites the nation across time and space, embodying its unity in its outward appearance, and re-establishing this unity in the greater purpose, and gathers civilizational lessons in discipline, equality, and collective responsibility.

**Part 9, Islam: And the System of Contemporary Life.** The book affirms that Islam does not clash with knowledge, nor is it hostile to reason, but presents a rightly guided, comprehensive vision that engages with the variables of the age, uniting between the fixed and the practical.

**Part 10, From Understanding to Action.** The book concludes that the true crisis lies not in the text, but in its application, nor in the Shari’ah, but in the human being, whose understanding has not been transformed into responsibility, for individual piety, without a collective consciousness, is not sufficient to help build reality.

**Conclusion.** The book concludes that the path to Allah is neither obscure nor complicated, but requires clarity of understanding, sincerity of deed, and steadfastness of method, for Islam was never, in the mind of its Founder, Allah, exalted is He above such a description, a burden upon life, but has always been a way to its flourishing and to guiding it, together.
